x2+(y−1)2=x2+(y+1)2⟹y=0.​

For real λ>0, squaring the two nonnegative moduli gives ∣z−i∣2=λ2∣z+i∣2. In Cartesian coordinates this is
(1−λ2)(x2+y2+1)−2(1+λ2)y=0.
(19)
Assume λ=1 and put h=(1+λ2)/(1−λ2). Dividing by 1−λ2 yields x2+y2−2hy+1=0. Since zz∗=x2+y2 and bz∗+b∗z=2Re(bz∗), the requested complex equation has
b=−i1−λ21+λ2​,c=1.​
(20)
Indeed these choices make the mixed term −2hy. Completing the square gives
x2+(y−h)2=h2−1=(1−λ2)24λ2​.
(21)
The Circles of Apollonius therefore have
centre zc​=i1−λ21+λ2​,radius ∣1−λ2∣2λ​.​
(22)
The radius is positive for the stated range. No spurious point at z=−i has been introduced: at that point the undivided equation would require 4=0. Positive λ<1 gives a circle above the real axis, while λ>1 gives one below it.

iii

Words: 72 Articles: 1
d OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 72
iii OurBigBook.com
No finite choice of b and c gives a line. The coefficient of zz∗=x2+y2 is fixed at one, so completing the square always gives a circle, a point, or the empty set. A general equation Azz∗+bz∗+b∗z+c=0 could describe a line when A=0 and b=0, but changing the fixed quadratic coefficient is not permitted here. A limiting sequence of increasingly large circles does not make any one of these finite equations a line.

Solution

Words: 150
a OurBigBook.com
Write f(x,y)=F(u,v) in the proposed local coordinates. The multivariable chain rule gives
fx​=2xFu​+2yFv​,fy​=−2yFu​+2xFv​.
(26)
Consequently
yfx​+xfy​=2(x2+y2)Fv​=0.
(27)
Away from the origin the Jacobian determinant is ux​vy​−uy​vx​=4(x2+y2)>0, so the inverse function theorem justifies these local coordinates. Therefore Fv​=0 and the local general solution is
f(x,y)=Φ(x2−y2).​
(28)
Substitution verifies the result: fx​=2xΦ′ and fy​=−2yΦ′, whose weighted sum vanishes.
There is a global qualification. The coordinate map is two-to-one, and a level set of x2−y2 has separate characteristic curve branches. A single profile on the entire plane does not follow without a branch-identification assumption. For example, take f=exp[−1/(x2−y2)2] on the wedge x>0, x2>y2, and zero elsewhere. This is smooth, satisfies the equation, and has different values at (1,0) and (−1,0) despite equal u. The characteristic components of a hyperbolic first-order equation explain this obstruction. At the origin the coordinate map is singular and the original equation reads 0=0; the boxed answer is the intended local form on a regular branch, or a global form under an additional identification of branches.

i OurBigBook.com
The first partial derivatives factor as
gx​=4x(2+x2−3y2),gy​=4y(2+y2−3x2).
(29)
If either coordinate vanishes, the other equation forces the other coordinate to vanish as well. If both are nonzero, subtracting the two bracket equations gives x2=y2, and then x2=y2=1. Thus the complete list of stationary points is (0,0) and the four points (±1,±1).
The Hessian matrix is
Hg​=(8+12x2−12y2−24xy​−24xy8+12y2−12x2​).
(30)
At the origin it is 8I, which is a positive-definite matrix. At the four other points its eigenvalues are 32 and −16, independently of the signs. The second-derivative test therefore gives
(0,0): strict local minimum, g=0;(±1,±1): saddle points, g=4.​
(31)
There are no local maxima. The minimum at the origin is not global, since g(t,t)=8t2−4t4→−∞ as ∣t∣→∞.

ii

Words: 130 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 130
ii OurBigBook.com
Within the requested first-quadrant square, the stationary points visible in the contour plot are the corner minimum (0,0) and the saddle (1,1). Near the origin, g≃4(x2+y2), so the low positive contours look like quarter-circles. Along either coordinate axis, g=4t2+t4 rises monotonically. Along the diagonal, g(t,t)=8t2−4t4 rises to 4 at t=1, returns to zero at t=2​, then becomes negative.
The saddle contour g=4 crosses at (1,1) and separates the central positive contours from the outer diagonal region. Negative contours occur toward (2,2), where g=−32, while the axis corners (2,0) and (0,2) have g=32. These checks determine both the contour ordering and the change of connectivity at the saddle; the figure shows these level sets.

Put L=5π/2. The curve tangent is r′=(−bsinθ,bcosθ,c). For the first line integral, the scalar triple product identity gives (a×r)⋅r′=a⋅(r×r′). Its cross product is
r×r′=(bc(sinθ−θcosθ), −bc(θsinθ+cosθ), b2).
(33)
The needed definite integrals are
∫0L​(sinθ−θcosθ)dθ=[−θsinθ−2cosθ]0L​=2−L,
(34)
and ∫0L​(−θsinθ−cosθ)dθ=[θcosθ−2sinθ]0L​=−2. Hence
I1​=bc(2−25π​)ax​−2bcay​+25πb2​az​.​
(35)
For the second line integral, substitute the curve into v2​⋅r′. The cubic terms combine to b3cosθ, leaving
v2​⋅r′​=b3cosθ+bc2θ2cosθ+2bc2θsinθ=dθd​[bsinθ(b2+c2θ2)].​
(36)
The fundamental theorem of calculus therefore gives
I2​=b(b2+425π2c2​).​
(37)
Both calculations retain the full path from θ=0 to 5π/2, rather than inadvertently closing the helix after one turn.

c OurBigBook.com
Direct calculation of the curl gives
∇×v1​=2a,∇×v2​=0.
(38)
Since a=0, the first vector field cannot be a gradient field: the curl of a gradient is zero. The second is a smooth polynomial field on all of the simply connected space R3, so its vanishing curl makes it a conservative vector field. A potential is also constructed explicitly in the next part. Thus v2​ is a conservative vector field and v1​ is not. A vanishing divergence alone, as for v1​, is a different property and does not establish conservativity.

By the spectral theorem for real symmetric matrices, choose the normalized eigenvectors to form an orthonormal basis. With Pn​=en​enT​, orthonormality gives Pn​Pm​=δnm​Pn​ and ∑n​Pn​=I. For every vector x, expand x=∑n​(enT​x)en​ and apply A:
Ax=∑n​λn​en​(enT​x).
(41)
Since this equality holds for every x, the spectral decomposition is
A=n=1∑N​λn​en​enT​.​
(42)
Each Pn​ is the rank-one orthogonal projection onto its eigenvector direction. In a degenerate eigenspace, normalized eigenvectors must be chosen mutually orthogonal; normalization alone does not guarantee this resolution of the identity.

The arrival phase has a uniform distribution over a cycle of length R. The no-delay phases occupy length R−r, so
P(S=0)=RR−r​=1−Rr​.​
(60)
Individual phase endpoints have probability zero. The model neglects clearance time and releases waiting vehicles together when the stop interval ends; the degenerate case r=R is interpreted as release at successive cycle boundaries.

Solution
Words: 89
ii OurBigBook.com
For a stop-phase arrival at time t, the delay is s=r−t. An interval of delays of width ds therefore corresponds to an interval of arrival phases of the same width, because ∣dt/ds∣=1. Its unconditional probability is ds/R. Hence the positive-delay part has density
p(s)={1/R,0,​0<s≤r,r<s≤R.​​
(61)
This ordinary density integrates to r/R, not to one: the remaining probability mass is at s=0. Thus S has a uniform distribution with an atom at zero, with mixing weight q=r/R. Conditional on a positive delay, the density would instead be 1/r on (0,r).

The graph of the positive-delay probability density function is a horizontal segment at height 1/R from s=0 to r, followed by zero from r to R. Values at individual endpoints do not affect probabilities. The separate atom 1−r/R at zero is not a finite-height part of this density graph.
The companion cumulative distribution function in the figure is FS​(s)=0 for s<0, FS​(s)=1−r/R+s/R for 0≤s<r, and FS​(s)=1 for s≥r. Its jump at zero displays the discrete part without confusing density height with probability mass.

P(S>0)=∫0r​Rds​=Rr​.
(62)
Adding the separate no-delay event gives
P(S=0)+P(S>0)=(1−Rr​)+Rr​=1.​
(63)
This is the normalization of a probability distribution with both discrete and continuous parts.

μ=E[S]=0(1−Rr​)+∫0r​Rs​ds=2Rr2​.​
(64)
This mean is r/R times the mean r/2 conditional on encountering a stop; using r/2 alone would omit the vehicles passing without delay.

Var(S)=3Rr3​−4R2r4​=12R2r3(4R−3r)​,σ=12R2r3(4R−3r)​​.​
(66)
The variance is nonnegative because 0<r≤R. Both μ and σ have units of time. At r=R the result reduces to R/12​, the standard deviation of a uniform distribution over one full cycle.

P(τ1​=0∣t)=Rr−t​.​

The original timeline below shows the three disjoint ranges of τ0​. The same idealized simultaneous-release convention as in part (a) is used.

If B arrives during the remaining pass phase, then r<t+τ0​<R, or r−t<τ0​<R−t. It passes immediately, so
τ1​=(t+τ0​)−r=τ0​−(r−t).
(68)
Because r−t>0, this is strictly between zero and τ0​. The phase interval has length (R−t)−(r−t)=R−r, giving
P(0<τ1​<τ0​∣t)=RR−r​.​
(69)

Solution

The remaining arrivals occur in the next stop phase: R≤t+τ0​≤R+t, or R−t≤τ0​≤R. B waits until R+r, while A departed at r, giving τ1​=R≥τ0​. This interval has length t, hence
P(τ1​≥τ0​∣t)=Rt​.​
(70)
Endpoint assignments do not affect probabilities. The three outcomes are exhaustive and satisfy
Rr−t​+RR−r​+Rt​=1.​
(71)
These are conditional probabilities for the stated fixed t; there is no additional averaging over A's arrival phase in the question.

Finally, holding W,θ fixed gives

Solution

i OurBigBook.com
On a connected domain, a vector field is a conservative vector field if and only if it is the gradient of a single-valued scalar potential, H=∇ϕ​. Equivalently, its line integral is path independent, or its integral around every closed curve is zero. For a continuously differentiable field on a simply connected domain, this is equivalent to ∇×H=0. Without the domain hypothesis, vanishing curl alone is only a local test and is not the necessary-and-sufficient global statement.

Words: 63 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 63
ii OurBigBook.com
Yes. For any sufficiently smooth scalar χ, the gauge transformation
G=G+∇χ​
(98)
leaves its curl unchanged because ∇×∇χ=0. This freedom is much larger than adding a constant vector: for example, χ=xy adds the nonconstant vector (y,x,0). Two vector potentials for the same field differ by a curl-free field; on a simply connected domain that difference is a gradient, while nontrivial topology may allow additional global freedom.

(99)
Its divergence is zero, as expected because the divergence of a curl is zero.

For a smooth oriented surface S with piecewise smooth boundary C=∂S and a continuously differentiable vector field G, the Stokes theorem states
∫S​(∇×G)⋅ndS=∮∂S​G⋅dr.​
(100)
The boundary orientation is fixed by the right-hand rule: curling the fingers along the positive boundary direction makes the thumb point along the surface normal. For an outward upper cap, its boundary ellipse is traversed counterclockwise when viewed from the positive z direction. The figure shows two possible caps with the same oriented boundary, anticipating the last part.

The integrand field is exactly the curl computed in part (a), so use its polynomial vector potential G=(z3,x3,y3)/3. The upper cap meets the plane z=0 in an ellipse. Since the parameters are only assumed nonzero, set a0​=∣a∣ and b0​=∣b∣ to use positive semiaxes. Its correctly oriented boundary is
r(t)=(a0​cost,b0​sint,0),0≤t≤2π.
(101)
On that boundary, Gx​=0 and dz=0, so only Gy​dy=x3dy/3 contributes. The Stokes theorem therefore gives
A​=∮C​G⋅dr=31​∫02π​(a0​cost)3(b0​cost)dt=3a03​b0​​∫02π​cos4tdt=3a03​b0​​43π​.​
(102)
The last integral follows by expanding cos4t=(3+4cos2t+cos4t)/8. Thus
A=4π​∣a∣3∣b∣=4π​a2∣ab∣.​
(103)
The result is independent of c. A sign check uses the divergence theorem: closing the cap with its base disk adds outward normal −z there. Since ∇⋅F=0, the cap flux equals ∫disk​x2dxdy>0, consistent with the boxed expression and its absolute values.

Solution

c OurBigBook.com
The modified upper surface has exactly the same ellipse at z=0 and the same boundary orientation. The field retains the global polynomial vector potential from part (a). By the Stokes theorem, both surface fluxes equal the same boundary line integral; the cap's height and interior shape do not enter. Hence
A=4π​a2∣ab∣.​
(104)
This is an instance of the fact that solenoidal flux depends on the oriented boundary, with the domain condition automatically satisfied by the smooth polynomial field on all of R3. When a,b are chosen positive, the formula simplifies to πa3b/4; the absolute-value form respects the original allowance of arbitrary nonzero signs.
